items.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I came up listening more to the Nat Cole kind of piano playing

ctx.x: When Wallace first introduced you to jazz repertoire, who were some of the artists that you feel influenced your direction?

No doubt, the Modern Jazz Quartet. I think the reason was because of John Lewis and the classical thing, and Milt Jackson and the blues. So, there it is, classical and gospel. Milt Jackson, gospel, right? So that was just a natural. But then, Oscar Peterson. Oscar Peterson beat me up. Whoa. It’s like getting on a bronco. I’m trying to hold on. I’m not even playing, but this guy – not only is he playing with such clean technique, but he’s swinging so hard at any tempo. A medium tempo, there he goes. A tempo that…

took me a while to get into Bud Powell and even longer to get into Thelonious Monk. In those early days, I guess I’m talking about the romantic piano players. Erroll Garner, George Shearing, Billy Taylor. But then I liked Red Garland, and I like Wynton Kelly, Phineas Newborn, Jr. There were some that didn’t have their own big name, but – Bill Evans.

items.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got to have dinner with him a couple of times.

ctx.x: How about, also associated with Chicago, but maybe a different generation, Fatha Hines?

Earl “Fatha” Hines was in my life because of my dad. Earl “Fatha” Hines, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson – my dad brought all that into my life, and that’s how – that’s also the Nat “King” Cole. If you go – if you follow Nat back as a piano player, you get into Teddy Wilson, you get into Earl “Fatha” Hines. To realize that he was one of the first piano players to not use stride a lot. Up until him, stride was the thing. He was one of the first piano players to take out the stride, just play chords, and his right hand was…
[end of tape 2; the recording again resumes in mid-sentence.]
